Q: How to go to implementation with mouse click? A:

I found a workaround using the alternativeDefinitionCommand setting for Java files with a single implementation.

This allows you to use Ctrl+Click twice (once to go to the definition, then in the next view Ctrl+Click it will take you to the implementation).

You can set this by going to:

  • Ctrl+, to go to Settings (UI)
  • Search for editor.gotoLocation.alternativeDefinitionCommand
  • Set to editor.action.goToImplementation

Or in your settings.json, add:

"editor.gotoLocation.alternativeDefinitionCommand": "editor.action.goToImplementation",

Q: SAMD11 I2C (SERCOM0) never leaves IDLE state A:

A few things to check specifically for custom PCB

I2C implementations with SAMD11:

1. Pull-up resistor value vs bus capacitance

4.7kΩ is on the high side for I2C. If your PCB

traces are long or you have multiple devices on

the bus, total capacitance may be causing slow

rise times. Try 2.2kΩ pull-ups and measure

SDA/SCL waveforms with an oscilloscope — you're

looking for clean transitions from 0V to 3.3V

within 300ns (Fast mode) or 1µs (Standard mode).

2. SERCOM pad mux verification

On SAMD11, SERCOM I2C requires specific PAD

assignments. SDA must be on PAD[0] and SCL

on PAD[1]. Verify your pinout in the datasheet

against your PCB routing — it's easy to get

SERCOM peripheral function mux wrong if using

a non-default pin mapping.

3. Check for floating bus condition

With nothing driving the bus, both lines should

sit at VCC (pulled high). If either line sits

at an intermediate voltage, you have a wiring

issue — check for unintended solder bridges

or wrong resistor values on your PCB.

4. IDLE state timeout

SAMD11 I2C master won't leave IDLE until it

detects a valid START condition. If the slave

address ACK is never received, it returns to

IDLE. Confirm slave address in your code

matches the device — check A0/A1/A2 hardware

address pins if your sensor has configurable

addressing.

What does your oscilloscope show on SDA/SCL

when you trigger a transaction?

Q: KEDA + Celery: Need Immediate Pod Scaling for Each Queued Task (Zero Queue Length Goal) A:

The core problem is a mathematical mismatch between your listLength target and how KEDA's HPA formula works.

KEDA feeds the queue depth into Kubernetes' standard HPA algorithm:

desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × (currentMetric / targetMetric))

With listLength: "1" and 1 pod running, when queue=1:

desiredReplicas = ceil(1 × (1/1)) = 1  ← no scale up!

KEDA only triggers a scale-up when the metric exceeds the target. You need a queue ≥ 2 before a second pod is requested, which is exactly the lag you're seeing.

Solution 1 — Set listLength: "0" (the correct fix)

triggers:
  - type: redis
    metadata:
      host: redis-master.namespace.svc
      port: "6379"
      listName: celery
      listLength: "0"   # ← change this
      activationListLength: "0"

With target=0, any non-zero queue depth immediately produces desiredReplicas = infinity, which KEDA caps at maxReplicaCount. In practice this means: 1 task queued → scale to max instantly. Combine with maxReplicaCount set to your actual concurrency ceiling.

Caveat: This is aggressive — every queued task tries to peg replicas to max. Pair it with a tight cooldownPeriod and a realistic maxReplicaCount to avoid thrashing.

Solution 2 — Use targetAverageValue mode (more precise)

Switch to the averageValue scaling model so each pod is responsible for exactly 1 task:

triggers:
  - type: redis
    metadata:
      host: redis-master.namespace.svc
      port: "6379"
      listName: celery
      listLength: "1"
      activationListLength: "0"
  advanced:
    horizontalPodAutoscalerConfig:
      behavior:
        scaleUp:
          stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0      # ← no delay on scale-up
          policies:
            - type: Pods
              value: 10                       # max pods to add per interval
              periodSeconds: 5               # matches your pollingInterval
        scaleDown:
          stabilizationWindowSeconds: 120    # keep your cooldown on scale-down

The key addition is stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0 on scale-up. By default Kubernetes averages metrics over a 5-minute window before scaling up — this is what causes the lag even when listLength math looks correct. Setting it to 0 makes scale-up decisions immediate.

Solution 3 — Fix Celery prefetching (often the real culprit)

Your config has --prefetch-multiplier 1, which is correct, but Celery still reserves 1 task per worker even while processing. This means the pod appears busy to the queue but isn't actually processing your new task yet.

Add --without-heartbeat and reduce the ack timeout:

command:
  - celery
  - -A
  - celeryapp.worker.celery
  - worker
  - --concurrency=1
  - --prefetch-multiplier=1
  - --without-heartbeat         # ← reduce broker chatter
  - --without-gossip            # ← reduce broker chatter
  - --without-mingle            # ← faster worker startup
  - --optimization=fair
  - --queues=celery

--without-mingle is particularly important here — without it, each new pod spends 1–2 seconds synchronising state with existing workers before pulling tasks, creating a visible delay even after KEDA has already scaled.

Recommended combined config

kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: celery-worker-scaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    kind: Deployment
    name: celery-worker
  pollingInterval: 5
  cooldownPeriod: 120
  maxReplicaCount: 10
  minReplicaCount: 1
  advanced:
    horizontalPodAutoscalerConfig:
      behavior:
        scaleUp:
          stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
          policies:
            - type: Pods
              value: 10
              periodSeconds: 5
        scaleDown:
          stabilizationWindowSeconds: 120
  triggers:
    - type: redis
      metadata:
        host: redis-master.namespace.svc
        port: "6379"
        listName: celery
        listLength: "1"
        activationListLength: "0"

Why true zero-queue is practically impossible

There's an irreducible floor here worth understanding: even with perfect KEDA config, you have:

  • KEDA polling interval: 5s (your config)

  • Kubernetes pod scheduling: ~2–5s

  • Celery worker startup + --mingle: 1–3s

Total minimum latency per task: ~8–13 seconds. You can get queue depth to 0 eventually for each task, but not instantaneously. If your requirement is truly real-time, consider pre-warming pods by keeping minReplicaCount higher, or switching to a thread-pool model (--concurrency=4) so existing pods absorb burst tasks before new pods are needed.

Q: Remap AltGr/CapsLock+[jkli] to arrows and preserve combination with modifiers such as Ctrl/Shift in A:

You can get AltGr to work with modifiers by using the built-in syntax with remap:

<^>!j::Down

<^>! is AltGr. My keyboard doesn't have AltGr key though, so it doesn't work for me. Please check if it works for you.

Alternatively, use >! for RAlt.

; Works on my keyboard which doesn't have AltGr
; Works with other modifiers
 >!j::Down

For CapsLock you'll have to use Custom Combinations like what you've been doing.

On my computer, CapsLock & j::MsgBox "Caps & j" doesn't toggle CapsLock though.

The docs does state that:

The prefix key loses its native function, unless it is a standard modifier key or toggleable key such as CapsLock.

If a hotkey would be activated by pressing the prefix key on its own, by default the hotkey is fired upon release, and is not fired at all if another key is pressed.

The prefix key loses its native function: In the above example, Numpad0 becomes a prefix key; but this also causes Numpad0 to lose its original/native function when it is pressed by itself. To avoid this, a script may configure Numpad0 to perform a new action such as one of the following:

Hence, you can try using these 2 lines together, CapsLock shouldn't toggle if used with j:

CapsLock::CapsLock
CapsLock & j::MsgBox "Caps & j"

If this doesn't work AND CapsLock is consistently toggled every time, then you can just get the script to automatically untoggle it for you:

CapsLock & j::
{
    MsgBox "Caps & j"
    SetCapsLockState !GetKeyState("CapsLock", "T")
}
